works.name: Don't Let Him Waste Your Time

podcast.title: Artistic Evolution Beyond Brit-Pop
podcast.body: As the Brit-Pop movement declined, Jarvis Cocker deliberately steered his artistic direction away from its confines, exploring new musical territories. He delved into an earlier interest in artists like Scott Walker, ultimately evolving into a "modern experimental singer," a style evident in albums like "This Is Hardcore." "Jarvis Cocker began to work in a totally different way, delving into that stage that he had liked so much at the beginning of being Scott Walker of those great charismatic classics."

podcast.title: Britpop Age Comparison
podcast.body: Jarvis Cocker is mentioned as being in his thirties during the Britpop era, contrasting with Vimo Galman who was 19, to illustrate the age diversity often found in musical styles, unlike the more age-homogenous grunge scene. "gente como Jarvis Coquer que tenía 30 y pico."

podcast.title: Connection to Gorillaz Creators
podcast.body: Jarvis Cocker of Pulp knew Jamie Hewlett. He also introduced Graham Coxon of Blur to Jamie Hewlett, which eventually led to Damon Albarn and Jamie Hewlett becoming acquaintances and later collaborating on Gorillaz. "So Jamie knew Jarvis Cocker of Pulp, obviously. And Jarvis was a maid of Graham Cox and a blur."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Early Ambition for Stardom
podcast.body: Jarvis Cocker's primary motivation for starting Pulp was not necessarily musical talent or grand musical aspirations, but rather an intense personal dream of becoming a "superstar." This ambition fueled his persistence through the band's challenging first 15 years, despite having "everything against him." "Jarvis Cocker is not someone who had great musical concerns or great musical talent, but rather the dream of a person who wanted to be a superstar and who had everything against him."

podcast.title: Iconic 90s UK Persona
podcast.body: Jarvis Cocker became an iconic figure in 90s Britain, known for his distinct "old school" Britishness. He possessed an eccentric and somewhat strange, yet highly charismatic and attractive personality, making him a captivating presence in interviews during the mid-90s. "Jarvis Cocker was one of those great British characters in the 90s."

podcast.title: Impact of Drug Addiction on Creativity
podcast.body: Following the success of "Different Class," Jarvis Cocker developed a severe cocaine addiction in 1997. This addiction, along with other internal band issues, led to a creative paralysis where he struggled to write new material, managing to produce only the song "Help the Aged" over several months. This period significantly impacted Pulp's ability to record their next album. "during a year, well, there are recordings of the concerts in 1997 of Palt that some are truly pathetic, that Jarvis Cocker ended up vomiting on stage here in Spain in one of the concerts."

podcast.title: Successful Solo Career
podcast.body: After Pulp, Jarvis Cocker embarked on an "incredible solo career," characterized by his continued charisma and unique artistic vision. "after this already Pulp is on a completely different path from Brit-Pop and would not look back after This Is Hardcore would come out We Love Life that also has nothing to do with Brit-Pop although it is more similar to This Is Hardcore but it follows Jarvis Cocker's personal path and then we would have the incredible solo career of Jarvis Cocker in which he is full of charisma."

podcast.title: Unsuccessful James Bond Theme Song Submission
podcast.body: Jarvis Cocker was approached to write a theme song for a James Bond film and did record a version, but it was ultimately rejected. This anecdote highlights a lesser-known aspect of his creative output and his willingness to explore diverse projects. "Jarvis Cocker was about to make one of the songs for one of the James Bond films but was finally rejected but he did record it."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Artist of a Generation Award (1996)
xref.body: Michael Jackson received this award at the Brit Awards on February 19, 1996, during which Jarvis Cocker of Pulp staged a protest by interrupting his performance. "On February 19th, 1996, Michael Jackson was on hand to pick up his Artist of a Generation Award."

xref.title: Departure from Pulp
xref.body: Russell Senior was a guitarist and violinist for Pulp, joining in 1980 and staying through their Britpop peak. He eventually quit the band, feeling annoyed that singer Jarvis Cocker (referred to as "Jarvis Pulp" in the transcript) was receiving all the attention. "But then he soured on the whole thing and was greatly annoyed that Singer Jarvis Pulp was getting all the attention. So he quit."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Pulp's "Common People" Comic Strip
xref.body: In 1995, Hewlett illustrated a comic strip based on the story of Pulp's song "Common People," which was included with the French version of the single and an Australian box set. This connection highlights his acquaintanceship with Pulp's Jarvis Cocker. "He also illustrated a comic strip in 1995 that was based entirely on the story told in this song by Pulp."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
